Multilinear Regression

V. Markos

2026-11-17

  • Our First Multilinear Regression Model!

Our First Multilinear Regression Model!

First, load our data and create a model of mpg against weight, HP and drat:

mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat, data = mtcars)
summary(mlm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.3598 -1.8374 -0.5099  0.9681  5.7078 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 29.394934   6.156303   4.775 5.13e-05 ***
## wt          -3.227954   0.796398  -4.053 0.000364 ***
## hp          -0.032230   0.008925  -3.611 0.001178 ** 
## drat         1.615049   1.226983   1.316 0.198755    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.561 on 28 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8369, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8194 
## F-statistic: 47.88 on 3 and 28 DF,  p-value: 3.768e-11

So, the computed model is:

\[mpg=29.394934-3.227954wt-0.032230hp+1.615049drat\] The interpretation of the above formula is as follows:

  • For 1000 lbs of additional weight, we run 3.227954 miles / gallon less ceteris paribus (c.p.).
  • For 1 H of additional HP, we run 0.032230 miles / gallon less (c.p.).
  • For a change of 1 in rear axle ratio, we run 1.615049 miles / gallon more (c.p.).
  • For the (fictional) case of a car with 0 weight, 0 HP and 0 rear axle ratio, we run 29.394934 miles / gallon.

In our context ceteris paribus means “all other parameters being the same”.

To begin with, observe that \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\) are good enough, accounting for more than \(80\%\) of the total variance in our data. But, as you might well see, our \(p\) values are not as strong as last time. Namely:

  • For weight, we have a \(p\) value of \(0.000364\) which is good enough.
  • For HP, we have a \(p\) value of \(0.001178\) which, again, is below common confidence thresholds of \(0.05\) or \(0.01\).
  • For rear axle ratio we see that there is a really weak \(p\) value of \(0.198755\), which means that there is a \(20\%\) chance that we make a type I error, i.e., we erroneously reject the null hypothesis that there is no effect of drat of mpg (or the other way).

Also, besides the fact that drat appears to not be correlated in this model, we also observe a weak coefficient between mpg and hp, namely, \(-0.032230\).

So, what is going wrong with this model?

Testing for Correlations

We should first test whether there are any correlations in our independent variables:

ivars <- mtcars[, c('wt', 'hp', 'drat')]
ivars_cor <- cor(ivars) # This computes Spearman's correlation
print(ivars_cor)
##              wt         hp       drat
## wt    1.0000000  0.6587479 -0.7124406
## hp    0.6587479  1.0000000 -0.4487591
## drat -0.7124406 -0.4487591  1.0000000

We should also compute the \(p\) values for each correlation:

# install.packages('Hmisc')
library(Hmisc)
## 
## Attaching package: 'Hmisc'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     format.pval, units
ivars_cor_p <- rcorr(as.matrix(ivars))
print(ivars_cor_p$P) # Get just the p-values
##                wt           hp         drat
## wt             NA 4.145827e-05 4.784260e-06
## hp   4.145827e-05           NA 9.988772e-03
## drat 4.784260e-06 9.988772e-03           NA

So, as we see here, all independent variables are somehow correlated with strong enough \(p\) values, which means that the multicollinearity assumption might not hold. In particular, drat appears strongly correlated with wt, which might imply that we should exclude one of the two variables. Also, there is a notable correlation between hp and wt, which also explains why we see such a small coefficient for hp in the above model.

We can also visualise the above using a correlogram:

# install.packages('corrplot')
library(corrplot)
## corrplot 0.95 loaded
corrplot(ivars_cor, method = 'circle')

Computing a New Model

In theory, larger values for drat should result to higher fuel consumption, i.e., lower mpg. Inversely, smaller values for drat should result to higher mpg. However, in our previous model the case was inverted since the regression coefficient was 1.615049 which is positive, that is, drat is found to positively affect mpg. One way to verify this is to also plot a correlogram including mpg, so:

corrplot(cor(mtcars[, c('mpg', 'wt', 'hp', 'drat')]), method = 'circle')

We are now going to create a compound index taking into account drat and hp together by multiplying those, i.e.:

cor_mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat + hp * drat, data = mtcars)
summary(cor_mlm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat + hp * drat, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.2292 -1.8974 -0.7182  0.9502  5.3868 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 17.13334    8.98518   1.907 0.067234 .  
## wt          -3.59247    0.79164  -4.538 0.000105 ***
## hp           0.07517    0.05983   1.256 0.219741    
## drat         5.02313    2.21859   2.264 0.031810 *  
## hp:drat     -0.02849    0.01571  -1.814 0.080835 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.463 on 27 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8546, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8331 
## F-statistic: 39.67 on 4 and 27 DF,  p-value: 6.208e-11

Above we added an interaction term, as we say, where we add, alongside drat and hp, also hp*drat, i.e., their product. This is typically done in cases where we are interested into quantifying any interaction between two or more of our independent variables. However, we should do so carefully, because adding such terms typically lowers the significance of other variables’ coefficients, as we saw above. If that happens, this means that doing so actually introduced more multicollinearity, i.e., made our model worse. So, this interaction, should, in principle, be ignored.

Maybe, a different approach, might be to just drop drat, to begin with, and see with what sort of model we end up with:

no_drat_mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(no_drat_mlm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -3.941 -1.600 -0.182  1.050  5.854 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 37.22727    1.59879  23.285  < 2e-16 ***
## wt          -3.87783    0.63273  -6.129 1.12e-06 ***
## hp          -0.03177    0.00903  -3.519  0.00145 ** 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.593 on 29 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8268, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8148 
## F-statistic: 69.21 on 2 and 29 DF,  p-value: 9.109e-12

Comparing this model with our first one, we see virtually no change, besides stronger \(p\) values, which means that, in general, we should drop drat from our analysis.

Now, besides \(p\) values and \(R^2\), we should also look at Normal Q-Q plots and the rest of the useful plots we saw last time:

plot(no_drat_mlm)

Starting with residuals vs fitted, we see a pretty much good picture, where residuals are nicely distributed. Also, the Q-Q plot seems to verify the normal residual distribution assumption. Also, we see that the scale-location plot is quite good, looking like randomly scattered points. The only plot that is a bit less good than the simple model we crafted last time is the residuals vs leverage plot, where we see that some observations have more leverage compared to our previous model and, also, residuals are a bit negatively distributed for lower values of leverage.

Trying A Different Approach

Another approach to handle correlations between variables is to create a new variable based on highly correlated ones and create a simpler model. In our case, out of wt, hp and drat, we saw that drat is maybe irrelevant to mpg on the presence of the others, so we dropped it. Also, we saw that wt and hp are quite positively correlated, so, we might create a new index by using both wt and hp and then use that to create a simple regression model. One simple approach is to center our values for wt and hp by subtracting their mean values and then add them, i.e.:

mwt <- mean(mtcars$wt)
mhp <- mean(mtcars$hp)
wt_hp_index <- (mtcars$wt - mwt + mtcars$hp - mhp)/2
index_data <- data.frame(mtcars$mpg, wt_hp_index)
colnames(index_data) <- c('mpg', 'wt_hp_index')
wt_hp_mlm <- lm(mpg ~ wt_hp_index, data = index_data)
summary(wt_hp_mlm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ wt_hp_index, data = index_data)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -5.5857 -2.1380 -0.9074  1.5370  8.1586 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 20.09062    0.67617  29.712  < 2e-16 ***
## wt_hp_index -0.13605    0.01985  -6.853 1.32e-07 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 3.825 on 30 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6102, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5972 
## F-statistic: 46.97 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 1.322e-07

Here, we get a solid \(p\) value, but our model explains much less of the variance. To see that, we can also plot the corresponding scatterplot:

plot(index_data$wt_hp_index, index_data$mpg)
abline(wt_hp_mlm, col = 'red')

plot(wt_hp_mlm)

So, for this model, we see that all metrics discussed above are more or less worse off than in the first and third models. Evidently, we should keep either the simple mpg ~ wt model or the multilinear mpg ~ wt + hp models, which do explain a lot of variance with most metrics being quite good.

Working with Real Data

Let us now briefly try to create some models on real data, in particular, the ESS-pol dataset we had extracted last time.

ess_pol <- read.csv('ess_pol.csv', header = TRUE, sep = ',')
head(ess_pol)
##   X ess_data.cntry ess_data.nwspol ess_data.netusoft ess_data.netustm
## 1 1             AT              90                 5              180
## 2 2             AT              90                 5              570
## 3 3             AT              30                 5               30
## 4 4             AT              15                 1             6666
## 5 5             AT              60                 5              120
## 6 6             AT             120                 5              120
##   ess_data.ppltrst
## 1                5
## 2               10
## 3                6
## 4                6
## 5                6
## 6                8

To begin with, we should clean all dummy values, i.e., 7777, 8888, 9999 and so on:

# We essentially look through each row, compute the sum of those that contain 9999 and keep only those which
# sum up to 0, i.e., those that do not contain 9999
for (v in c(5555, 6666, 7777, 8888, 9999)) {
  ess_pol <- ess_pol[rowSums(ess_pol == v, na.rm = TRUE) == 0, ]
}

Next, we create a simple MLM:

ess_lm <- lm(formula = ess_data.ppltrst ~ ess_data.nwspol + ess_data.netusoft + ess_data.netustm, data = ess_pol)
summary(ess_lm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = ess_data.ppltrst ~ ess_data.nwspol + ess_data.netusoft + 
##     ess_data.netustm, data = ess_pol)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -5.719 -1.477 -0.305  1.654 93.890 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)        4.1981335  0.3701901  11.340  < 2e-16 ***
## ess_data.nwspol   -0.0002429  0.0001452  -1.672  0.09444 .  
## ess_data.netusoft  0.2238868  0.0760692   2.943  0.00325 ** 
## ess_data.netustm   0.0002787  0.0001214   2.295  0.02174 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.395 on 38481 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.000514,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.0004361 
## F-statistic: 6.597 on 3 and 38481 DF,  p-value: 0.0001881
plot(ess_lm)

This is evidently a bad model, mostly because we have not taken into account country plus some further data cleaning is required. So, you can have fun yourselves if you want to.
